title: OnPrem / Airgapped - GPU drivers, artifact delivery & offline licensing deep dive
header:
Date: 2026-03-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 64 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Lena Ortiz (Atlas - Head of ML), Samir Khan (Atlas - Infra), Priya Mehta (Atlas - Sec), Tom Alvarez (Atlas - Procurement)
summary: Deep technical session focused on on-prem / air-gapped delivery: offline artifact packaging, GPU driver licensing and installation, KV cache persistence, batching strategies, quantization tradeoffs, and VPC networking constraints. Agreed next steps: Redwood to provide artifact delivery checklist, offline license manifest, driver compatibility matrix, and schedule a 4-hour runbook workshop on-site or via secure VPN. Customer to share hardware inventory and procurement timelines.
topics: runtime performance: KV cache, batching, quantization
action_items: Maya Chen - Send artifact delivery checklist + tarball md5sums + secure transfer options by 2026-03-05
Ravi Patel - Share GPU driver compatibility matrix (CUDA/CUDNN/NVIDIA driver versions) and installation runbook by 2026-03-06
Atlas - Share hardware inventory (GPU model, NICs, OS) and estimated procurement dates - owner: Samir Khan - due 2026-03-09
Jordan Lee - Prepare offline license manifest and instructions for HSM-backed key import - due 2026-03-07
Priya Mehta - Confirm compliance requirements (SOC2 / FIPS / customer KMS) and list of audits to satisfy - due 2026-03-10
next_steps: Redwood to provide secure S3 presigned + removable media options for artifact transfer

transcript:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out the time. We're going to dive into artifact delivery and offline licensing, plus the driver questions we saw in the questionnaire.
[00:20] Lena (Atlas - Head of ML): Thanks, Maya. We're particularly worried about the airgap flow — we can't have outbound egress from the prod vlan and procurement wants to know what we actually need to buy.
[00:35] Ravi (Redwood SE): Yep, understood. We'll cover three main things: artifact packaging and transfer, driver/offline license keys, and the runtime perf knobs — kv cache, batching, quant.
[00:50] Samir (Atlas - Infra): Quick context — our initial plan is two racks, each with 2x A100 80GB, Ubuntu 22.04, Mellanox CX6 100Gb, and HSM appliance for keys.
[01:10] Jordan (Redwood SE): Perfect, that aligns with our tested configs. Note: small differences in NIC firmware can affect NVLink topology discovery — we can share a firmware checklist.
[01:35] Priya (Atlas - Security): Also need to confirm the offline licensing process — can we import licenses into our HSM? Is there a signed manifest?
[01:50] Maya: Yes, we support HSM-backed key import; we'll provide an offline license manifest signed by Redwood, and a verification step. We'll also include md5/sha256 for artifact integrity.
[02:10] Lena: Great. Can you explain the artifact size? Our procurement is worried about how many USB drives vs. shipping disks.
[02:25] Ravi: The base runtime tarball is around 8-12GB compressed; model weights vary — a 70B quantized model is ~60GB with int8, larger for fp16. We typically provide a model bundle per version. For airgap we can give a differential patch to save bandwidth.
[02:50] Samir: So for our initial two-model set (redwood-rev-70B and a smaller 13B), estimate about 80-90GB total compressed?
[03:05] Jordan: Sounds right with quantized weights. We'll send a manifest with exact sizes. Also: during transfer we recommend signed tar + checksum and a separate license file.
[03:20] Priya: On the license file, is there an offline activation token tied to hardware? We can't have a cloud callback.
[03:35] Maya: We support both hardware-tied and time-bound offline licenses. For hardware-tied, we'll provide a signed blob you import into your HSM which unlocks the runtime. No outbound callback required.
[03:55] Tom (Atlas - Procurement): Any vendor verbiage we should include for procurement? Export compliance?
[04:10] Maya: We'll include a short procurement pack: license terms, support SLAs, and export compliance notes. We'll flag any components that need export controls.
[04:25] Lena: Let's pivot to GPU drivers — we ran into a blocker where the driver installer needs kernel headers and curl, but our airgapped host doesn't have package manager access.
[04:40] Ravi: Two options: provide a full offline driver bundle with prebuilt dkms modules for common kernels, or provide an offline installer plus a small set of deps. Prebuilt is faster but we need exact kernel version.
[05:05] Samir: We're standardizing on Ubuntu 22.04 LTS with kernel 5.15.x but some older nodes are 5.13.
[05:20] Jordan: If you can standardize kernel patch level for the cluster it simplifies prebuilt modules. Otherwise we supply the full driver source + dkms and a build runbook — that requires gcc and make on nodes.
[05:40] Priya: Are there signed driver requirements for FIPS?
[05:50] Ravi: The driver binary itself is unsigned but kernel module signing can be enforced. We document steps to sign the built module with your key before you load it. That integrates with Secure Boot workflows.
[06:10] Lena: Can you walk through the offline license import step? What files do we need to hand to our HSM team?
[06:25] Maya: We'll deliver a license package: license.json (signed), license.sig, and a license_importer binary that runs in an airgapped environment to push the blob into the HSM's import API. The importer supports PKCS11 for many HSMs.
[06:45] Samir: Will the importer need network access to Redwood?
[06:55] Jordan: No, everything is signed and verified locally; the importer only verifies signatures using Redwood's public key. We'll also provide instructions for offline verification.
[07:15] Priya: Is the public key pinned? How do we rotate keys later?
[07:25] Ravi: We provide a key rotation process: you'll receive a rotation manifest and a verified chain; rotation can be done with a scheduled maintenance window and the importer will validate chain of trust. We'll document rollback steps.
[07:45] Lena: Switching to runtime perf — our SLO is 50ms p95 for short chat turns on the 13B model and 200ms p95 for the 70B for synchronous calls. Is that realistic on our planned hardware?
[08:10] Jordan: For 13B on a single A100 80GB with optimized kernels and batching disabled for low latency, 50ms p95 is achievable for 1-2 concurrent requests, but tail latency increases with NVMe thrash and OS scheduling. For 70B you'll likely need model sharding across two GPUs or quantization to int8 with specialized kernels to hit 200ms.
[08:45] Samir: We were hoping to keep everything on single-GPU to simplify ops.
[08:55] Ravi: Single GPU 70B is tough even with 80GB — KV cache and activation memory eat up space. Quantization helps (8-bit grouped or nf4), but you trade off some quality. We can provide quality regression tests.
[09:15] Lena: Tell us more about KV cache persistence — if we warm the cache on a dev box and then move to prod, can we pre-load KV?
[09:30] Jordan: Yes, we support prefix/KV snapshotting. You can serialize KV cache and load it at runtime during startup. For airgapped setups we recommend creating and shipping a KV snapshot as part of the artifact bundle, but note that snapshot size depends on token count.
[09:55] Priya: Is the KV snapshot encrypted at rest?
[10:05] Ravi: By default it's encrypted using the customer's KMS/HSM keys; we'll provide instructions to wrap the snapshot with your key material.
[10:20] Tom: For benchmarking, what telemetry do you need and can that remain internal (no outbound)?
[10:35] Maya: We can do fully offline runs and you can share artifact logs via encrypted transfer. If you want Redwood to ingest telemetry for support, we support a push model where you export logs and share via secure transfer — never requires outbound from prod.
[10:55] Lena: On batching — how do you recommend we balance throughput vs. latency? Our use case has mixed short chat and heavy embedding workloads.
[11:10] Jordan: Use latency-sensitive routes with batching disabled or small batch sizes and a dedicated low-latency pool. For embeddings or bulk inference, route to a high-throughput pool with larger batch windows. We'll provide autoscale policies and suggestions — e.g., 5-20ms batching window for low-latency, 50-200ms for throughput jobs.
[11:40] Samir: How does batching interact with KV cache? If you batch many different prefixes, you lose cache locality right?
[11:55] Ravi: Correct. Workload-aware batching groups similar prefix lengths; our router can bucket by prefix hash to preserve KV locality. For airgapped, you can enable that policy in the config.
[12:15] Priya: Quantization question — we saw an 8-bit config recommended, but some of our team argue for nf4; what's the tradeoff?
[12:30] Jordan: NF4 reduces memory slightly vs int8 but is sometimes faster on certain kernels. Quality varies by model. For 70B nf4 + kernel optimizations can hit a good latency/cost sweet spot; we provide model-quality diffs so you can validate.
[12:55] Lena: Do you have precomputed regressions for common benchmarks?
[13:05] Maya: Yes, we have a quality benchmark suite (we'll share a link to the repo in the follow-up) and precomputed diffs for recommended quantization profiles.
[13:20] Tom: On networking — the hosts will be in a private VLAN, no internet egress. Can Redwood's private control plane still perform rollouts?
[13:35] Ravi: For Private deployments we give you a control plane that can be either Redwood-hosted (requires egress) or self-hosted. For airgapped you use the self-hosted control plane; rollouts happen via artifact pushes and signed manifests.
[13:55] Priya: Is RBAC and SSO supported in self-hosted mode?
[14:05] Jordan: Yes, SAML/SSO can be configured against your IDP in the self-hosted console; all configs are in the private control plane package.
[14:20] Lena: Regarding driver licensing — are there vendor fees or offline license checks for the GPU drivers themselves?
[14:35] Ravi: NVIDIA driver is covered by their license; we don't relicense it. Offline licensing here refers to Redwood runtime and model usage. We'll include a section calling out any vendor-specific instructions for drivers.
[14:55] Samir: Some of our nodes are old and may need older drivers; can Redwood runtime run with older CUDA versions?
[15:10] Jordan: We test across a matrix. We'll share the matrix — older CUDA/CUDNN combos may reduce perf or disable certain kernels. We recommend staying on supported LTS stacks.
[15:30] Lena: On the installation runbook — can you outline the full steps we should expect in the workshop?
[15:40] Maya: Sure: pre-checks (firmware, kernel, packager deps), driver install (offline method), runtime install, import license into HSM, model load and KV warm, run microbenchmarks, validate p95/p99, and capture logs. We'll provide a checklist and runbook with commands.
[16:05] Tom: How long does a full install take? Our ops scheduling needs an estimate.
[16:15] Ravi: For an experienced infra team, a single node with prebuilt modules is ~45-60 minutes; building drivers on-node can add 1-2 hours. For a 4-node rack expect 4-6 hours including verification. That's why we suggested a 4-hour workshop for a single rack.
[16:40] Lena: Are there any special kernel tunables you recommend for throughput? IRQ affinities, huge pages?
[16:50] Jordan: Yes — enable hugepages (1G preferred for large models), tune irqbalance or pin interrupts to cores with CPU isolation for process threads, and set RPS/XPS for NIC. We'll share a sysctl and isolcpus template.
[17:10] Priya: Audit logs — does the offline deployment still provide the same level of per-request audit logging for compliance?
[17:20] Maya: Yes. The audit log subsystem writes to local encrypted storage and you can export logs. For higher retention we offer optional archival modules to export to your object store via secure transfer.
[17:40] Samir: For quality regression testing, do you provide tools to run A/B between quantized and fp16 models?
[17:50] Jordan: Yes, we have an eval harness that runs both versions against your prompt set and outputs diff metrics. We'll package that in the artifact bundle for airgapped use.
[18:05] Lena: Edge case — what if a node loses access to HSM after license import? Any fallback?
[18:20] Ravi: We have a grace period feature: a signed offline token that allows the runtime to operate for a configurable grace window if HSM unavailable. But long-term you need the HSM keys; we'll document recommended HA for HSM.
[18:40] Tom: Procurement question — any maintenance windows required for license rotations?
[18:50] Maya: Rotations typically require a brief restart of the runtime component to load new keys — 30-90s. We'll provide zero-downtime patterns when you have a multi-node pool.
[19:05] Lena: Ok let's talk benchmarks. Can you run a micro-benchmark for 70B quantized with batch=1 and measure 95th lat on our same NIC?
[19:20] Jordan: Yes — we can run bench with your supplied rack or supply a synthetic that approximates your network. For accurate results we need the hardware inventory and firmware levels.
[19:35] Samir: We'll export lspci, nvidia-smi -q, kernel version, and NIC firmware.
[19:45] Maya: Awesome, please attach to the ticket. We'll run a baseline and return numbers plus config suggested changes.
[20:00] Priya: Any gotchas we should know about with offline updates? e.g., model hot-swap while maintaining traffic.
[20:15] Ravi: We support canary deploys in self-hosted mode via manifest rollouts — you push the signed model bundle and the router can shift traffic gradually. For airgapped this is file-based but the flow is the same.
[20:30] Lena: A quick thing — some of the names in our questionnaire were mis-typed, you referenced 'KV cache' as 'KV cash' in the notes. Please confirm the actual field names in the runbook.
[20:45] Jordan: Good catch — we'll standardize naming in docs.
[21:00] Tom: On pricing — does offline deployment cost more because of support and artifacts?
[21:10] Maya: Typically Private deployments include a platform fee plus a one-time artifact/offline licensing facilitation fee and optional on-site support. We'll send a pricing sheet.
[21:25] Lena: Anything else on compliance? FIPS, SOC2 items we need to check?
[21:35] Priya: We're specifically checking for FIPS and ability to provide signed attestations for patch levels.
[21:45] Ravi: We'll include an attestation pack and the SOC2 summary. For FIPS you'll need to configure crypto modules to FIPS mode — we have documented steps.
[22:05] Maya: Okay let's recap and assign owners.
[22:10] Jordan: Recap: Redwood to send artifact bundles, checksums, driver matrix, license importer, and runbook. Atlas to send hardware inventory and schedule the workshop.
[22:25] Samir: We'll target sending inventory by Monday.
[22:35] Tom: Procurement will review pricing and come back with PO questions by next week.
[22:45] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the checklist and a shared secure transfer plan. Thanks everyone.
[23:00] Lena: Thanks all.
[23:10] (call ends)

Notes: Transcript contains occasional mis-hearings and shorthand; speakers sometimes overlap. Links/Artifacts mentioned: artifact-manifest.csv (to be shared), runbook.tar.gz (secure transfer), driver-matrix.xlsx (attachment).
